proposals.relationship: Uses Appadurai’s account of colonial enumeration to examine how sexual classification differentiated subject populations (2000).
proposals.evidence_note: Own abstract and printed6 cite his colonial-imagination work alongside Cohn, Inden and Sinha. A specific analytical resource, with the other scholars’ credit retained; not proof of personal mentoring or an exclusive origin. Appadurai’s original chapter remains unread.

proposals.relationship: Uses Foucault’s terminology to frame the accumulation and classification of knowledge in British colonial governance (2000).
proposals.evidence_note: Own printed6 expressly invokes archaeology of knowledge while developing the counting argument. This records Levine’s particular conceptual use; it does not certify equivalence with Foucault’s complete method, establish a formative debt or identify an unread original edition.

proposals.relationship: Draws on Hall to resist unitary readings of racial and gender difference and to interpret claims of English dominance.
proposals.evidence_note: Own2000conclusion16 explicitly values Hall’s1993 warning about shifting otherness;2003introduction7 also cites Hall on English dominance. The latter note’s body is absent from the preview, so no exact edition is guessed. These resources coexist with Levine’s later particular questions about Civilising Subjects; underlying Hall works unread.

proposals.relationship: Credits Burton with reading and debating the complete manuscript of Prostitution, Race, and Politics before publication (2003).
proposals.evidence_note: Own acknowledgment ix jointly credits Burton, Jim Epstein and Doug Peers with that intellectual work. Shared credit is preserved; no claim of sole influence, formal supervision or reading only inferred from friendship. Other section readers retain separate collective credit.

proposals.relationship: Invokes Wolfe’s call for a unified historical field while arguing that representation and material consequences should be studied together (2003).
proposals.evidence_note: Own introduction10–11 explicitly uses Wolfe in defending the combination of political, administrative, military, social and cultural history. This does not automatically classify the book as adopting every settler-colonial model. Note28’s body and the Wolfe original are unread; exact title or edition not invented.

proposals.relationship: Uses Said’s connection between comparative literature and imperial authority to question supposedly neutral national units of comparison (2003).
proposals.evidence_note: Own chapter1,16 places Said alongside Robert Gregg’s separate criticism of transhistorical national labels. Resource limited to this argument; not adoption of all Orientalism claims. Note3’s body is absent from the preview and the Said original is unread.

proposals.relationship: Questions the separated metropolitan and colonial narratives and the relative absence of women in Civilising Subjects, as Hall records (2003).
proposals.evidence_note: Hall’s own533–534 and536–537 attributes both questions jointly to Levine and Thomas Holt. Hall defends her narrative choice and focus on imperial men while admitting that more could have been done with women. The original commentaries and Hall’s monograph are unread; the criticism is expressly recipient-reported and does not cancel Levine’s positive Hall resources.

proposals.relationship: Develops cross-colonial comparison that treats nations and racial labels as historical products while retaining differences among imperial settings.
proposals.evidence_note: Selected2003chapter1,15–17 compares four distinct colonial settings connected through governance and migration; the2014authorial abstract later explains both comparative rewards and universalist risks. A particular contribution to the combined world/global/connected-history entry, not an assertion that comparison and connection are identical methods or that she founded the field. Whole books/article and cited originals unread.
